sections.label: Drug abuser and inmate statistics
sections.summary: Over 3,000 drug abusers are caught yearly since 2011, about 1,000 new, and almost one in three inmates is reconvicted within two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Since 2011, more than 3,000 drug abusers are caught every year, out of which, about 1,000 are new.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Among the new drug abusers in 2016, close to two-thirds were below 30 years of age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In 2015 and 2016, the Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) admission increased when overall penal admission had decreased.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Per the most recent statistics, almost one in three inmates is convicted again within two years.

sections.label: Leaders on Singapore drug laws
sections.summary: Teo Chee Hean and K Shanmugam defended Singapore's tough drug laws, citing cannabis seizures rising 125% in 2014 and cannabis becoming the second most abused drug among new abusers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: As Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean said at an ASEAN Ministerial Meeting, I quote, "We should also prepare well for the international debate on a new global action plan to tackle drugs. … We must not let softer approaches that allow the harm from drug use to spread..." Minister K Shanmugam correctly said in defence of Singapore's tough laws at last year's UN General Assembly, "For us, the choice is clear.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2014, the amount of cannabis seized spiked by 125% from 15 kg in 2013 to 35 kg in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: For the first time, cannabis became the second most commonly abused drug among new abusers in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: That year, there was about a 26% increase in cannabis seized from 35 kg to 44.3 kg.

sections.label: Cannabis seized increase 2016
sections.summary: The amount of cannabis seized increased by another 22% from 2015 to 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The data showed that over the entire year, the amount of cannabis seized increased by another 22% from 2015 to 2016.

sections.label: Drug quantities feeding abusers
sections.summary: Two hundred and fifty grammes of meth feeds 185 abusers for a week, and 15 grammes of diamorphine sustains about 180 abusers for a week.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Two hundred and fifty grammes of meth feeds 185 abusers for a week and 15 grammes of diamorphine sustains about 180 abusers for a week.

sections.label: Arrests of abusers under 30
sections.summary: The number of abusers arrested under the age of 30 has increased by about 20% since 2014.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The number of abusers arrested under the age of 30 has increased by about 20% since 2014.

sections.label: Cannabis seized yearly increases
sections.summary: In 2014, 2015 and 2016, the amount of cannabis seized increased each year by 125%, 26% and 22% respectively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2014, 2015 and 2016, the amount of cannabis seized increased each year by 125%, 26% and 22% respectively.

sections.label: Number jumped in 2012
sections.summary: In 2012, the number jumped by almost 42% to 2,472.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2012, the number jumped by almost 42% to 2,472.

sections.label: Reviewing MDA legal powers
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether drugs should be allowed to destroy Singaporeans' lives and proposes re-examining whether the MDA needs a further review to ensure it has the legal arsenal and muscle to deter drug supply into Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Do we allow drugs to destroy the lives of Singaporeans or do we say, "No, not on our shores!"?

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Therefore, Madam, I propose that we re-examine whether the MDA needs a further review to ensure that it is constantly equipped with the legal arsenal and muscle it requires to deter the supply of drugs into Singapore.

sections.label: Online drug arrests and suggestions
sections.summary: Arrests for buying drugs and drug-related paraphernalia online rose from 30 in 2015 to 201 in 2016, a 570% increase, and six suggestions are made, including creating an aggravated offence for Internet-facilitated acts, an offence for Internet recruitment to traffic drugs under enhanced punishment, another punishment tier for traffickers targeting persons under 30 and using the Internet, and defini

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Our agencies have worked hard to catch such abusers and hold them responsible for their actions." The number of people arrested for buying drugs and drug-related paraphernalia online increased significantly from 30 in 2015, to 201 in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: That is a 570% increase over the span of one year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: For example, an aggravated offence could be created where any act in the series of acts leading up to the eventual sale or potential sale of the drug was performed through the medium of the Internet or any social media platform.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The fourth suggestion is to make an offence the act of recruiting, via the Internet, to traffic drugs using the Internet and to bring that new offence under an enhanced punishment regime similar to that for recruiting young offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The fifth suggestion is to have another tier of punishment for drug traffickers who possess the aggravating factors of (a) targeting persons under 30 years and (b) using the Internet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The sixth suggestion is that of defining Internet broadly in the MDA to include websites, social media platforms and applications.

sections.label: Distinguishing addiction and trafficking
sections.summary: First, we must distinguish between addiction and trafficking.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: First, we must distinguish between addiction and trafficking.

sections.label: DRC recidivism and task force
sections.summary: The current DRC recidivism rate is 30.1%, more than half of drug abusers arrested each year were repeat abusers, and in 2011 a Task Force on Drugs was formed, leading the Singapore Prison Service to implement the Community Rehabilitation Centre and Enhanced Drug Rehabilitation Regime.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The current recidivism rate for DRC is 30.1%, almost one in three of our inmates is coming back through the door within the first two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Furthermore, each year, more than half of the drug abusers arrested were repeat drug abusers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2011, a Task Force on Drugs was formed to "tackle the drug abuse situation." Through its recommendations, the Singapore Prison Service implemented the Community Rehabilitation Centre (CRC) and the Enhanced Drug Rehabilitation Regime.

sections.label: Phoenix Multisport example
sections.summary: One example is Phoenix Multisport in the United States, where recovering, like-minded drug abusers who want to stay sober do exhilarating physical activities together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: One example is Phoenix Multisport in the United States, where recovering, like-minded drug abusers who want to stay sober do exhilarating physical activities together.

sections.label: Japanese programme and web-based version
sections.summary: Research found the Japanese programme raises drug abusers' awareness and motivation, and in 2016 researchers attempted a web-based version with videos, websites and calendars.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Research on the effectiveness of the Japanese programme found that it "increases a drug abuser's awareness of problems, their motivation for treatment and serves as preparation for group therapy." In 2016, researchers attempted to develop a web-based version, which included videos adapted from cognitive behavourial therapy, websites linked to addiction support services and self-monitoring colour-coded calendars, to enhance motivation.

sections.label: US opioid overdoses and cannabis legislation
sections.summary: In 2015 US prescription and illicit opioid overdoses multiplied four times since 1999, and cannabis legislation saw more traffic accidents in Washington and Colorado.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2015, in the United States, overdoses on prescription and illicit opioids multiplied by four times since 1999.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Since the legislation of cannabis, there has been an increase in traffic accidents and fatal traffic accidents in Washington state and Colorado, which have legalised cannabis.

sections.label: Cannabis exposure in young children
sections.summary: In 2016 a journal reported cannabis exposure rates in young children, many toddlers, rose 150% since 2014 when recreational marijuana products went on sale legally.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2016, the Journal of the American Medical Association Pediatrics reported that "the rates of cannabis" exposure in young children, many of them toddlers, have increased 150% − this is for toddlers − since 2014 when recreational marijuana products went on the market legally." All of these are totally preventable.

sections.label: Cannabis industry growth projections
sections.summary: Cannabis is touted as America's fastest growing industry, projected to grow from $3.4 billion in 2015 to over $10 billion by 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Cannabis is touted to be "the fastest growing industry in America".

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: It is projected to grow from $3.4 billion in 2015 to more than $10 billion by 2019.

sections.label: MOE Science syllabus learning material
sections.summary: The first suggestion is to include clear, informative learning material in the MOE Science syllabus detailing the ills and harmful effects of experimenting with drugs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The first suggestion is that we include clear and informative learning material in our MOE Science syllabus, which should detail the host of ills and harmful effects of experimenting with drugs.

sections.label: Fighting pro-drug propaganda
sections.summary: The speaker urges liberty to use the best weaponry, warns of a social abyss drugs can bring, and hopes the House will fight pro-drug propaganda.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: We should be at liberty to use the best weaponry for this crucial battle on our shores.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: We can build and share a common prosperity or we can disintegrate into a common poverty of spirit, a potential social abyss, which drugs can bring, insidiously, stealthily.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: I hope, today, this House will fight against the pro-drug propaganda.

sections.label: New drug abusers arrested 2016
sections.summary: The number of new drug abusers arrested in 2016 rose by 3% compared to the previous year.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: First, the number of new drug abusers arrested in 2016 increased by 3% compared to the year before.

sections.label: Online drug arrests and youth attitudes
sections.summary: Online drug-related arrests rose from 30 in 2015 to 201 in 2016, mostly aged 20 to 39, and a 2016 NCADA survey found under-30s more open-minded towards drugs than in 2013.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The number of people arrested for buying drugs and drug-related items through online means increased significantly from 30 in 2015 to 201 in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The majority of them are between the ages of 20 and 39.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: These numbers are worrying, especially when a survey conducted by the National Council Against Drug Abuse (NCADA) in 2016 found that young people below the age of 30 were more open-minded towards drugs, compared to similar findings in 2013.

sections.label: Call to stop drug use in institutions
sections.summary: The speaker calls for CNB, the Police, the Health Promotion Board and Institutes of Higher Learning to stop drug use and abuse in educational institutions, even if numbers are small.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: While I must state that these are only two of his many friends who otherwise lead drug-free and healthy lifestyles, I am calling for CNB, the Police, the Health Promotion Board and our Institutes of Higher Learning to go all out to stop such drug use and abuse in our educational institutions, even if the numbers are small and seemingly insignificant.

sections.label: Curbing online drug peddling
sections.summary: The speaker hopes CNB and IMDA can curb online drug peddling more effectively and take tougher enforcement action against online drug buyers.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In addition, I hope CNB and Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) can find ways to curb online peddling of drugs more effectively and take tougher enforcement actions on those who are buying drugs online.

sections.label: Countering pro-cannabis claims
sections.summary: The speaker calls for medical professionals and research experts to verify pro-cannabis claims and curb the perception that small daily drug doses are fine, with all parties playing roles.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What is equally worrying is the callous claims by some pro-cannabis and pro-marijuana proponents that small amounts of cannabis use is perfectly alright, or that there are medical conditions, such as glaucoma or Parkinson's disease, that can be managed through daily doses of cannabis or marijuana or ganga, whatever name it is known as.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: We would also need the help of medical professionals and research experts to verify such claims and, more importantly, to curb the incorrect perception that small doses of drug use on a daily basis are perfectly fine.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: We would need all parties to come together to do this to help ourselves and our future generations − parents, schools, the Government, popular personalities − all have important roles to play.

sections.label: US states legalising marijuana
sections.summary: In 2016, nine US states including California, Florida and Massachusetts passed laws allowing regulated medical or recreational marijuana use, and 44 states have legalised some form of drug use.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As many Americans went to the polls in 2016 to decide between Donald Trump and Hilary Clinton as their next President, a parallel vote took place on the legalisation of marijuana.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This resulted in nine states in the US, including California, Florida, Massachusetts, passing laws that allowed for either regulated medical or recreational marijuana use.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Today, 44 states in the US have legalised some form of drug use.

sections.label: Portugal less punitive drug policies
sections.summary: The writer noted Portugal adopted less punitive drug possession policies over a decade earlier without significant increases in drug use, harm or crime compared to punitive-law countries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The writer also reflected on countries like Portugal, which adopted less punitive policies towards drug possession more than a decade earlier and, in doing so, had not experienced any significant increase in drug use, drug-related harm or crime, compared to countries with punitive laws.

sections.label: Israel medical marijuana research
sections.summary: The New York Times reported Israel led medical marijuana research from the 1960s, with 25,000 citizens holding permits for cancer, epilepsy and other diseases, expected to grow.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Late last year, the international New York Times reported that Israel has been a leading player in medical marijuana research as early as the 1960s and that 25,000 of its citizens today hold permits to use medical marijuana to ease symptoms of cancer, epilepsy and other diseases, with the number expected to grow rapidly.

sections.label: Legalisation creating consumer industries
sections.summary: A Business Monitor article said growing recreational marijuana legalisation creates new consumer industries, especially food and beverage, with derivatives possibly added to beer, chocolates and candy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To that end, a recent Business Monitor online article notes that with the growing legalisation of marijuana for recreational use, entirely new industries for consumer-related companies will be created, including transport and through social media.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It assessed that while medical marijuana will be an important part of the market, recreational use of marijuana will create new opportunities for consumer industries, especially food and beverage, with derivatives of marijuana potentially added to beer, chocolates and candy.

sections.label: Global trends and Singapore drug control
sections.summary: The writer said global trends suggest Singapore will find it harder to keep drugs out and away from children amid seismic cultural shifts in attitudes worldwide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What the global trends suggest, and I turn to the language in the Motion, is that Singapore will find it even more difficult to keep drugs out of the country and in the consciousness of our children and people, in view of the seismic cultural shifts in attitudes towards drug use for medical and recreational purposes in many jurisdictions around the world.

sections.label: Singapore sticking to anti-drug policy
sections.summary: The writer said Singapore can and should stick to its time-honoured strong anti-drug policy given the evolving global environment, unique circumstances and success keeping drugs out of schools.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At this point, Singapore can and should stick to its time-honoured position of a strong anti-drug policy, in view of the still evolving global environment, our unique circumstances and because we have been able to get a handle on the drug problem and successfully kept drugs out of our schools.

sections.label: Cannabis arrests and permissive laws
sections.summary: The writer cited rising cannabis abuser arrests in the CNB 2016 report and a Lancet Psychiatry article finding permissive or decriminalised territories saw increased teenage and young adult drug abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The rise in the arrest of cannabis abusers, as reported in the CNB's drug situation report of 2016, may portend such a trend.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to Lancet Psychiatry, in a 2015 article, which revealed annual and repeated cross-sectional surveys on medical marijuana laws and adolescent marijuana use in the US from 1991 to 2014, almost a 25-year period, it found territories which decriminalised illicit drugs or where the laws were generally permissive, saw an increase in drug abuse among teenagers and young adults.

sections.label: Rehabilitation and drug education
sections.summary: The Government will step up education about drug abuse while stepping up rehabilitation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Stepping up rehabilitation is the right thing to do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, in view of the new global approach towards drugs, the Government will have to significantly step up education about the slippery slope of drug abuse and drug abuse per se.

sections.label: US drug overdose statistics
sections.summary: US National Institute on Drug Abuse statistics show over 50,000 overdose deaths in 2015 and a doubled death rate from 2002 to 2015.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: If we look at the statistics from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, in the year 2015, there were over 50,000 deaths from drug overdose in America.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In America, the death rate from overdose has more than doubled from 2002 to 2015.

sections.label: Early policy choices' long shadow
sections.summary: Policy choices at the beginning can set the tone for decades, so Singapore must be careful when asked to tolerate drugs.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: You can see it in many countries around the world.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: And this has deep lessons for us in Singapore because policy choices at the beginning can set the tone for decades afterwards.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It means a bad choice, an unwise choice, if it cannot be rolled back, will cast a very long shadow for what comes after, for our children and our grandchildren.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: We need to care and that means we need to be careful when people call upon Singapore to be tolerant of drugs, to condone drugs.

sections.label: Helping drug-affected families recover
sections.summary: While taking a tough stand against drug peddlers, Singapore must help affected families recover and give their children a fair start.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Again, disadvantaged by drugs; drugs promoting inequality, poisoning families, damaging the next generation.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, even as we take a tough stand to prevent drug peddlers poisoning our fellow Singaporeans and their families, we also need to look very carefully at how we can help these families recover, ensure their children still have a fair start in life.

sections.label: Speaker's opposition to capital punishment
sections.summary: The speaker supports tough laws but does not support capital punishment as a demonstration of them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I will not want to impose my moral position on this, but I think there are also issues with regard to this matter that I hope we can have more discourse on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I agree that it is important to have tough laws, but I do not believe that capital punishment, as a demonstration of the tough laws and resolution to fight against drug problems, is something that I can support.

sections.label: Harven Segar conviction overturned
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal overturned Mr Harven Segar's drug trafficking conviction, with two of three judges favouring acquittal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Just a few weeks ago, our Court of Appeal overturned the conviction of Mr Harven Segar, who was found guilty of drug trafficking by the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Two of the three judges thought that the Court should acquit the accused, while the third judge thought otherwise.

sections.label: Presumption and guilt without proof
sections.summary: Prof Michael Hor states that where the presumption is employed, an accused can be found guilty and executed without proof beyond reasonable doubt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As Prof Michael Hor has pointed out, "where the presumption is employed there can be no doubt that an accused person can be found guilty and executed in the absence of proof beyond reasonable doubt".

sections.label: Co-accused statements and due process
sections.summary: Prof Hor says investigation practices, including use of co-accused statements as sole basis for conviction, cast doubt on due process in capital cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Furthermore, what goes on during the investigation process is especially important because the statements of the co-accused persons can be used against the accused and can also form the sole basis of a conviction without corroborating evidence, even if the statements are subsequently retracted at the trial by the co-accused.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, in Prof Hor's view: "all these rules and practices taken together must at least cast some doubt on whether there is sufficient due process for the conduct of capital cases." Sir, if every other advanced criminal justice system in the world has convicted the wrong person, there is no reason to think that Singapore is immune to the problem.

sections.label: Deterrence data and enforcement
sections.summary: The passage asks whether conclusive data proves the death penalty deters drug trafficking, and notes CNB accepts active enforcement is the best strategy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But if we cannot sufficiently show that the death penalty yields more than a marginal deterrence effect or provide any objective data and evidence, we also have to ask ourselves whether it is necessary, or indeed fair, for us to create a whole new class of victims by carrying out those punishments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, do we have good and conclusive data and information that can prove beyond doubt that the death penalty and, by extension, such tough laws, would deter drug trafficking.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In fact, Sir, it appears, and is accepted by CNB itself, that it is active enforcement, both internally as well as joint border operations by our efficient CNB, that remains the best strategy towards disrupting the activities of drug syndicates and in reducing the supply of drugs from entering our borders as much as possible.

sections.label: Social and economic structures, rehabilitation
sections.summary: The passage questions whether gaps in social and economic structures, not insufficient punitive punishment, cause the drug problem, and says rehabilitation should also be for traffickers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is a question of the sufficiency of our social and economic structures to ensure that individuals have the social and economic means and support to enable them to lead a dignified and meaningful life such that there is little incentive for them to abuse drugs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is most telling when in 2015, out of the 1,400 individuals that were placed in the various drug rehabilitation centres (DRCs), 821 individuals had only Secondary school education, 308 individuals had only Primary school education and six individuals did not have any education at all.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Perhaps the profile of drug abusers might give us some indication that it is in the inadequacy and gaps in our social and economic institutions, rather than the failure of not having implemented more punitive punishment on drug consumption and drug trafficking that the problem lies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It goes without saying that if we are unable to effectively reduce the demand for drugs, the supply of drugs will continue to creep into our borders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I also want to raise another point − that rehabilitation should also be for drug traffickers and not just for the users.

sections.label: Arts programme and inmate rehabilitation
sections.summary: Ms Peggy Ferroa describes how inmates on an arts programme spend six hours daily rehearsing and reflecting, gaining confidence and helping others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to Ms Peggy Ferroa, the Arts Educator who worked with them, "Inmates on the programme spend at least six hours a day on week days rehearsing, planning ahead for performances or reflecting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If their minds are occupied with things that require concrete outcomes that they know they can do well in, it is likely that they spend less time thinking of ways to beat the system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: When their time is meaningfully spent and they are able to reach their personal goals, they gain confidence and start to think about what they can do for others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Some inmates in the programme have come up with educational workshops using drama for other inmates." Yes, Arts is powerful in helping the rehabilitative process, of building that resilience in them; to face change, to make change, to be the change themselves.

sections.label: Sustainable programmes build soft skills
sections.summary: The passage states the programme builds soft skills and resilience for return to society, and such programmes must be sustainable, not short workshops.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But the programme builds very important soft skills, as well as resilience, which will serve them well when they go back to society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These programmes must not be short workshops but sustainable ones that would focus on the process.

sections.label: MP on helping drug offenders
sections.summary: A former MP said help can be given to drug offenders but they can never be real fathers or husbands to them.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: At one point, the then Member of Parliament of Ulu Pandan, none other than Dr Vivian Balakrishnan himself, made a point and I also remember this, that we can give them as much help as we can but we can never be real fathers or real husbands to them.

sections.label: UN 2016 World Drug Report
sections.summary: The 2016 UN World Drug Report estimated one in 20 adults, a quarter of a billion people aged 15 to 64, used at least one drug in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: In the 2016 World Drug Report published by the United Nations Office of Drugs and Crime, it was estimated that one in 20 adults, or a quarter of a billion people between the ages of 15 and 64 years, used at least one drug in the year 2014 alone.

sections.label: Economic cost of drug abuse
sections.summary: Drug abuse costs the economy close to $200 billion annually, including crime, lost productivity and healthcare, making a drug-tolerant society too costly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Beyond this, drug abuse and addiction also impose a high cost to the economy, estimated at close to $200 billion annually by the National Institute of Drug Abuse.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: This includes costs related to crime, loss of work productivity and healthcare expenditures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: From an economic perspective, a drug-tolerant society is too high a cost for any society to bear.

sections.label: Children living with drug-dependent parents
sections.summary: Over 2.2 million children live with a parent dependent on illicit drugs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Because of that, over 2.2 million children live with a parent who is dependent on illicit drugs.

sections.label: Global Drug Survey online purchases
sections.summary: A survey of over 100,000 Internet users in 50 countries found drug purchases via the Internet rose from 1.2% in 2000 to 25.3% in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: A global survey, entitled Global Drug Survey, has surveyed more than 100,000 Internet users, 75% of whom had taken illegal drugs, in 50 countries in late 2014.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: This survey suggested that the proportion of drug users purchasing drugs via the Internet had increased rapidly from 1.2% in 2000 to 4.9% in 2009, then to 16.4% in 2013 and, most recently, 25.3% in 2014.

sections.label: Singapore online drug arrests rise
sections.summary: CNB statistics showed arrests for buying drugs and paraphernalia online rose about 600%, from 30 people in 2015 to 201 in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: In Singapore, statistics provided by CNB showed an increase of about 600% in people arrested for buying drugs and drug-related paraphernalia online, from 30 people in 2015 to 201 people in 2016.

sections.label: Tough drug penalties as deterrence
sections.summary: The passage argues that stiff penalties signal Singapore's zero-tolerance stance and should continue to deter illicit drug use.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: A strong system of laws with stiff penalties may be an unpleasant but crucial element in our battle against drug abuse.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: I believe that the tough penalties strongly and clearly signal Singapore's zero- tolerance stance towards the use of illicit drugs and we should continue to apply tough laws to deter illicit drug use.

sections.label: DRC recidivism rates
sections.summary: Two-year recidivism rates of persons released from DRCs fluctuate close to 30%, based on Singapore Prison Service statistics.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: The two-year recidivism rates of persons released from DRCs fluctuate close to 30%, based on statistics provided by Singapore Prison Service (SPS).

sections.label: Mentoring, education and deterrence
sections.summary: A Swedish study showed mentoring reduces recidivism by about 4% to 10%, and the passage suggests studying Germany's toy-free kindergarten approach.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: A study conducted for the Swedish National Council of Crime Prevention showed that mentoring at-risk individuals can help to reduce the likelihood of recidivism by about 4% to 10%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: We must also consider teaching the dangers of drug abuse at an early age.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: It was reported that kindergartens in Germany have started an innovative way of strengthening children against addictive behaviours through a toy-free project, in which children will be placed in a toy-free environment for a short period in the day.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Perhaps MOE can study the feasibility of such an approach to be used in our local context.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Thankfully, this figure is also much lower than many other countries, but we must not be complacent and we must keep this figure as low as possible, in fact, if we can, towards zero.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: We must do so through education, rehabilitation and, inevitably, deterrence, which means retaining the stiff penalties that we have in Singapore.

sections.label: Drug supply and access
sections.summary: Older ex-offenders said staying clean is harder now due to drug oversupply, more online and offline purchase avenues, and fallen prices.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The older ex-offenders confirmed for me that it is much harder for a drug addict today to stay clean because there is an oversupply of drugs in the market and it is true that they have many more avenues, online and offline, to purchase their drug of choice and prices have, indeed, fallen.

sections.label: Stable housing for rehabilitation
sections.summary: The most consistently raised issue was the need for stable accommodation and a supportive community, as early housing access reduces re-offence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The first and most consistently brought-up issue was the need for stable accommodation and a supportive community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is perhaps the most important factor to pay attention to if we are serious about rehabilitation, because extensive international research does show that early access to stable housing is one of the most critical factors that reduces re-offence.

sections.label: Rental flat sharing rules
sections.summary: Rules require two people to share one rental flat, so a former drug addict often rooms with another former drug addict.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Rules currently require two people to share one rental flat and, as circumstances will have it, a former drug addict will often end up rooming with another former drug addict.

sections.label: Long-term imprisonment for drug abusers
sections.summary: Hard-core drug abusers who cannot break the habit after repeated DRC treatment face LT1 of five to seven years and LT2 of seven to 13 years on re-offending.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For hard-core drug abusers who cannot break the habit after going through repeated DRC treatment, they are subjected to long-term imprisonment laws known as LT1 of between five and seven years, and when they re-offend, LT2 of between seven and 13 years.

sections.label: Objectives of Long-Term Imprisonment laws
sections.summary: The Long-Term Imprisonment laws aim to give society greater security and safety, deter drug abuse, and reduce crimes by drug addicts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The stated objectives of the Long-Term Imprisonment laws are to (a) provide greater security and safety to the rest of society; (b) deter individuals from continuing to abuse drugs; and (c) reduce the crimes committed by drug addicts.

sections.label: Extending halfway house detention periods
sections.summary: Some halfway houses believe the current last six to eight months of detention is too short and request extending it to one-and-a-half to three years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The strong punitive element of the LT1 and LT2 schemes must be counter-balanced with equally strong restorative elements.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Prisons Halfway House Scheme currently allows offenders without strong family support to spend their last stage of detention at a halfway house and offenders only spend an average of the last six to eight months of their detention there.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Some of the halfway houses I spoke to believe that this period may be too short to yield sustainable results.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: They have requested that, for better rehabilitative outcomes, it might be more useful to consider extending the period of detention that offenders can serve out in halfway houses to one-and-a-half, and even two to three years.

sections.label: Studies on programmes and recidivism
sections.summary: The ground requests Government-commissioned follow-up studies on housing needs, Prison School and in-prison programmes to help VWOs design better interventions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Follow-up studies tracking how housing needs, Prison School and other in-prison programmes impact employment rates and recidivism rates can give useful feedback to the VWOs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, the request from the ground is for the Government to commission studies that can provide the social sector more information to design better interventions.

sections.label: SkillsFuture for prisoners and ex-offenders
sections.summary: The passage asks whether a SkillsFuture vision and roadmap exists for lifelong learners in prisons and halfway houses.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Is there a SkillsFuture vision and roadmap for our lifelong learners in our prisons and halfway houses because I believe there are unique strengths and talents that our former drug addicts and ex-offenders do bring to the table?

sections.label: Leadership programme for ex-offenders
sections.summary: The passage suggests considering a leadership programme that talent-spots high potential former drug addicts and ex-offenders for social work-based skills.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But he is also right in pointing out there is a unique career opportunity here for ex-convicts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It might be worth considering a leadership programme that talent-spots high potential former drug addicts and ex-offenders to pick up social work-based skills that can enable them to support rehabilitative work in the future.

sections.label: Prison programme procurement and rehabilitation
sections.summary: A request for the Government to refine prison programme procurement to avoid fly-by-night vendors and favour long-term rehabilitation partnerships.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Their request is for the Government to consider refining the procurement process for prison programmes to guard against fly-by-night vendors who may pitch on programming contracts because it is another way to make a buck, rather than an opportunity to change a life.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As one programming provider stated very passionately to me, rehabilitative work that impacts so many lives should not be judged by the same matrixes of cost-effectiveness and novelty for change that we use to decide between contractors for chairs and tables.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I believe, for rehab programmes, it would be far more impactful to invest our taxpayers' money on long-term re-collaborative partnerships with providers that have a heart to commit to long-term rehab goals with the Singapore Prison Service.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A strong anti-drug stance paired with an equally strong pro-rehabilitation stance is an unusual policy combination in the world.

sections.label: Global heroin and illicit drug use
sections.summary: The World Drug Report states heroin consumption reaches 340 tonnes and almost 246 million people aged 15 to 64 use illicit drugs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: According to the World Drug Report, heroin consumption alone amounts to a staggering 340 tonnes and it is estimated that a total of almost 246 million people between the ages of 15 and 64, use illicit drugs.

sections.label: Singapore strict drug laws
sections.summary: Singapore's strict laws against drug consumption and trafficking have kept the country safe over the years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: In Singapore, our strict laws against drug consumption and trafficking have kept us safe over the years.

sections.label: Younger Singaporeans open to drugs
sections.summary: The National Council Against Drug Abuse reported more Singaporeans below 30 are open-minded about experimenting with drugs than a few years ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: The National Council Against Drug Abuse reported that many more of our younger Singaporeans below the age of 30 are now open-minded about experimenting with drugs as opposed to a few years ago.

sections.label: Second most widely used drugs
sections.summary: Their proliferation and easy availability make them the world's second most widely used drugs, exceeding heroin and cocaine, per the World Drug Report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Their proliferation and easy availability have made them the second most widely used drugs in the world, with levels exceeding those of heroin and even cocaine, so says the World Drug Report.

sections.label: Combating drug trade and capital punishment
sections.summary: An urge for the Government to combat drugs at source and target drug barons, while noting a moral dilemma over capital punishment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: I, therefore, urge the Government to do whatever is in its power to combat the drug problem at the source and also step up efforts to target the drug barons, the people who truly benefit exclusively from this illicit trade and yet are unremorseful at the fate of their helpless and often hapless runners who take on all the risks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: I must state very clearly at this point that I believe that capital punishment has been one reason that has kept us free from the worst of the drug problems that have plagued other countries, but I also have a strong personal moral dilemma in not wanting capital punishment to be enforced, especially when the ultimate perpetrators of the crime are often not the ones standing frightened at the gallows.

sections.label: Singapore drug laws and death penalty
sections.summary: The speaker credits Singapore's Police, Government and society, and welcomes 2012 amendments lifting the mandatory death penalty for certain drug trafficking and murder convictions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: But in Singapore's example, it is a strong, trustworthy and effective Police force, an incorrupt system of Government, a general intolerance of drug culture and a fair society where no one needs to resort to drugs as a first recourse for problems they face in life.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: I, therefore, welcome the 2012 amendments to our laws such that the mandatory death penalty for those convicted of drug trafficking or murder was lifted under certain specific conditions, with discretionary powers provided to judges to sentence such offenders to life imprisonment.

sections.label: Dignity and reintegration of drug abusers
sections.summary: The passage says drug abusers should be valued in their dignity and reintegrated into society through schemes, centres and halfway houses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: We cannot fall into the injustice of classifying them as if they were objects or broken junk; rather, they should be valued and appreciated in their dignity in order to be cured.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: They continue to have, despite their crimes, more than ever, dignity as persons." There is a lot of good work done by the Youth Enhanced Supervision Scheme, community rehabilitation centres, drug rehabilitation centres and our halfway houses, but society itself must be able to see our drug abusers beyond their mistakes and ensure that they do not just recover but also reintegrate into society and, therefore, have no reasons to return to drugs.

sections.label: Keeping Singapore drug-free
sections.summary: The passage says tough deterrent measures, targeting international gangs, community uplift and rehabilitation should keep Singapore safe, and supports new offences for online synthetic drug sales.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Singapore has remained relatively drug-free and we should endeavour to remain so and do whatever we can to do so.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Tough deterrent measures have kept us and our families safe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Targeting international criminal gangs and ensuring the uplift of vulnerable communities outside of Singapore and coupled with a robust rehab and reintegration regime – these will continue to keep us safe for the long haul.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He suspects that the numbers of persons purchasing synthetic drugs online will rise in the coming years.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I support the hon Members' suggestion of including new offences within the Misuse of Drugs Act which are aimed at these new ways for kingpins to peddle in drugs and to take decisive action against them.

sections.label: Rehabilitation for young first-time offenders
sections.summary: The passage states rehabilitation should often dominate sentencing for young first-time offenders, including probation or reformative training, not only the DRC.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For young, first-time offenders, inclusive of drug offenders, rehabilitation should often play a dominant role in determining the appropriate sentencing option.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Rehabilitation does not only mean sending an offender to the DRC.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In deserving cases, it can and should involve, Sir, probation or reformative training.

sections.label: Lapse of probation order
sections.summary: The passage states that if any conditions are not met, the probation order lapses and the probationer faces real jail time.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If any of those conditions are not met, the probation order lapses and the probationer has to face real jail time.

sections.label: Ridzuan's probation sentence
sections.summary: The passage states Ridzuan was convicted and sentenced by the District Judge to two years' probation, six months intensive and 18 months supervisory.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Ultimately, Ridzuan was convicted and sentenced by the District Judge and placed under two years' probation, six months of which were intensive, 18 months of which were supervisory.

sections.label: Court rulings on drug charges
sections.summary: Judge of Appeal Chao held it was vitally important not to view an accused's actions through lenses of someone familiar with drug trade practices.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In a Court of Appeal case, Judge of Appeal Chao held that "it was vitally important not to view the actions and words of an accused person in a case like this in the lenses of someone who is familiar with the practices of the drug trade, unless there are facts warranting that conclusion." With young first-time Singaporean drug offenders, we cannot assume that all of them are familiar with the practices of the drug trade.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That was only one of two cases just held last month by the High Court and the Court of Appeal where the charges were found to be unsubstantiated and the cases were ultimately found to be unwarranted.

sections.label: Rehabilitate-first approach for young offenders
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Ministry would support a rehabilitate-first approach towards drug trafficking for young first-time drug offenders.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Third, would the Ministry support a "rehabilitate-first" approach towards drug trafficking for young first-time drug offenders?

sections.label: Sensitisation training for CNB investigators
sections.summary: The passage asks whether CNB investigators and prosecutors should receive sensitisation and diversity management training to take a rehabilitate-first approach.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Three, should CNB investigators and misuse of drugs prosecutors be sent for sensitisation training and diversity management training so that when they first meet or deal with young offenders, they take a "rehabilitate first" approach instead of an approach which tends towards "prosecute at all costs"?

sections.label: Singapore drug abuse incidence
sections.summary: The incidence of drug abuse in Singapore is one of the lowest in the world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The incidence of drug abuse in Singapore is one of the lowest in the world.

sections.label: Rising young drug users
sections.summary: The passage states the rising number of young drug users below 30, who tend to be more affluent and use cannabis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The first is that of the rising number of young drug users below the age of 30.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This was a bit different because the typical profile of many of the other drug offenders who use heroin – and many of the other offenders are from the lower income groups – and they use drugs like heroin and meth which are a lot more damaging.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But the young users tended to be from a different social profile, including more affluent people, and they are using more cannabis.

sections.label: Falling abuse rates over study
sections.summary: Over a 20-year study, alcohol abuse fell from 42% to 5%, smoking from 23% to 3%, and cannabis use from 17% to 5%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Over the course of the 20-year study, the rate of alcohol abuse fell from 42% to 5%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The rate of cigarette smoking dropped from 23% to 3% and the rate of people who use cannabis fell from 17% to 5%.

sections.label: Online drug peddling arrests
sections.summary: Online drug peddling arrests rose from 30 in 2015 to 201 in 2016, and the speaker suggests stronger penalties and more action against sellers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The second issue which the CNB highlighted was online drug peddling.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This has risen from 30 arrests in 2015 to 201 in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Although the numbers are still small, the total rise is very significant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I agree with Mr Christopher de Souza's suggestions for stronger penalties and enhanced penalties if drugs arer peddled online.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I also note from the CNB report that most of the arrests were against people who were buying drugs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I would suggest that CNB take additional steps against those who are selling drugs, maintaining websites and are in any way part of this dark net.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: They are difficult to detect but, once detected, I think harsh penalties should be taken.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: While we strengthen our fight against drug consumption and ensure that people do not consume drugs in the first place, we must remember that almost 60% of drug abusers arrested are repeat offenders.

sections.label: DRC family visits
sections.summary: From 2014 to 2016, only about a third of DRC inmates received two family visits per month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: From 2014 to 2016, only about a third of DRC inmates received two family visits per month.

sections.label: DRC and LT2 recidivism rates
sections.summary: In 2013 the recidivism rate was 28.3% for DRC inmates and 42% for LT2 inmates; in 2014 it was 30.1% and 36.5%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In 2013, the recidivism rate for DRC inmates was 28.3% and for LT2 inmates, it was 42%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In 2014, the recidivism rate for DRC inmates was 30.1% and for LT2 inmates, it was 36.5%.

sections.label: Counselling for inmates' families
sections.summary: The speaker asks about developing more counselling programmes for families of inmates before release and a programme for children to spend a day behind bars with parents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can we also look into developing more counselling programmes for families of inmates even before their release from prison, to help their families to be better prepared to receive them upon their release and to support them in leading drug-free lifestyles?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: As I have suggested during the COS debates, can we consider introducing a programme where children get to spend a whole day behind bars with their parents?

sections.label: Reaching families during incarceration
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether resources exist to reach out to families during the first week of their loved ones' incarceration.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Do we have the resources to ensure that we reach out to them during the first week of incarceration of their loved ones?

sections.label: Family-centric rehabilitation approach
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether MHA will consider spearheading a unified national family-centric rehabilitation process, citing the 2014 Taskforce on Youth and Drugs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will MHA consider spearheading a unified national approach towards a family-centric rehabilitation process?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I believe we should draw inspiration from the Taskforce on Youth and Drugs in 2014, convened then by Mr Masagos Zulkifli.

sections.label: Rehabilitation action plan for drug-offenders
sections.summary: A similar targeted national action plan should be drawn up to rehabilitate all drug-offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: A similar targeted national action plan should be drawn up towards rehabilitating all drug-offenders.

sections.label: CNB set up in 1971
sections.summary: CNB was set up in 1971 to tackle this.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: To tackle this, CNB was set up in 1971.

sections.label: Heroin abusers and Operation Ferret
sections.summary: In the early 1970s less than 10 heroin abusers were arrested a year, but after CNB and Operation Ferret, 26,000 abusers had been arrested by February 1978.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In the early 1970s – mark this – we were arresting less than 10 heroin abusers a year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We could have kidded ourselves and believed that that was the true situation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But after we set up CNB and after we started Operation Ferret, by February 1978, 26,000 abusers had been arrested.

sections.label: 1993 DRC recidivism rate
sections.summary: In 1993, the DRC recidivism rate was 73%.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In 1993, our DRC recidivism rate was 73%.

sections.label: UNODC 2014 drug abuser estimate
sections.summary: UNODC estimates in 2014 that there are nearly 250 million drug abusers in the world.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: UNODC estimates in 2014 that there are nearly 250 million drug abusers in the world.

sections.label: Commercial motive for legalisation
sections.summary: Opponents of legalisation like Singapore are not financed, while a huge commercial motive drives legalisation in many countries.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Those who oppose legalisation, those who take a stand similar to Singapore's, if you look at the material, you would not want to look at them again because no one is financing them.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: There is a huge commercial motive for legalisation and that is driving this in many countries.

sections.label: Regional drug situation background
sections.summary: The passage states the region is near the Golden Triangle, the second largest opium source, and is the fastest growing meth market.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: That is the international situation; that is the background.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I have said this before, we are near the Golden Triangle, which is the second largest opium source in the world.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Our region is the fastest growing meth market.

sections.label: CNB new psychoactive substance seizures
sections.summary: CNB seized over 3.5 kilogrammes and 4,000 tablets of new psycho-active substances in the past two years, falsely marketed as legal and safe.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: CNB, for example, in the past two years, has seized more than 3.5 kilogrammes and 4,000 tablets of new psycho-active substances, which have been falsely marketed as both being legal and safe.

sections.label: Arrested abusers under 30
sections.summary: Last year, 40% of those arrested were abusers and were less than 30 years old.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Last year, 40% of those who were arrested were abusers, were less than 30 years old.

sections.label: United Against Drugs Coalition launch
sections.summary: CNB will launch the United Against Drugs Coalition later this month and review how it puts across messages.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: CNB will launch United Against Drugs Coalition later this month and also review the way it puts across messages.

sections.label: Cannabis recipient arrest seizure
sections.summary: Within hours, CNB arrested the intended recipient and seized more than one kilogramme of cannabis.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Within a matter of hours, CNB arrested the intended recipient and seized more than one kilogramme of cannabis.

sections.label: Information led to trafficker arrests
sections.summary: The information provided has contributed to the arrest of almost 90 drug traffickers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The information provided has contributed to the arrest of almost 90 drug traffickers.

sections.label: Drug quantity for death penalty
sections.summary: The death penalty threshold is possession of enough heroin to supply 180 people for seven days.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The quantity of drugs that you need to have in your possession before the death penalty kicks in, presumptions kick in, is enough heroin to supply 180 people for seven days.

sections.label: Lives saved by fewer arrests
sections.summary: Lower arrest numbers over 20 years mean tens of thousands of lives saved, perhaps 40,000 to 50,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Even if you take the lower end of those figures, say, 3,000 now and 6,000 then.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: That is 3,000 less per year, over a period of 20 years and assuming it came down, you are talking about tens of thousands, maybe 40,000, 50,000 lives saved because our enforcement ability has not gone down but we are arresting less people.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Every person not arrested who has not become an abuser is a life saved.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, we have saved maybe 40,000 or 50,000 lives or maybe more.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: If all things were equal between the 1990s and today, we were arresting 6,000 to 7,000 then, the number should be higher now, because we are wealthier now.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The drug production has increased, it has become more of a multinational enterprise, so perhaps, it should have been doubled; we should be arresting 15,000 people or maybe 18,000 people.

sections.label: Suffering caused by drug traffickers
sections.summary: For every person who brings in drugs, several hundred people suffer.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: And I do not want them to suffer and I do not want more people to suffer as a result of someone making a cynical calculation between his life and getting a few hundred ringgits.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, for every one person who brings in the drugs, there are several hundred people who suffer.

sections.label: Social and economic institution gaps
sections.summary: The speaker asks for clarification on which social and economic institution gaps causatively lead to drug abuse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, I am not sure quite exactly what you mean.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: And you tell us, of the 1,400 individuals that were placed in 2015 in DRC, 820 had Secondary education, 300 had Primary education, six no education.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: And you said this gives some indication that it is the inadequacy and gaps in our social and economic institutions, rather than the failure of not having implemented more punitive punishment on drug consumption and drug trafficking that the problem lies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: What are the inadequacy and gaps in our social and economic institutions that lead to this drug abuse?

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I hope you will clarify exactly what social institutions you are referring to, what economic institutions you are referring to, and what gaps and, causatively, how they relate to the drug problem.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Tell me what the gaps are in the social institutions, which ones, what are the gaps in economic institutions and how do they really lead causatively to these 821 people getting into drugs.

sections.label: Going soft on drugs
sections.summary: Going soft is what will happen, and the Deputy Leader is asked to move the exemption.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: You go soft, that is what will happen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
sentences.text: Deputy Leader, would you like to move the exemption?

sections.label: Public support for death penalty
sections.summary: REACH polls show 80% supported retaining the death penalty and 82% saw it as an important deterrent.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: When REACH did a poll last year, 80% supported retaining the death penalty, 10% wanted to abolish it, 10% had no position or refuse to answer.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Also, 82% agreed that it was an important deterrent to keep Singapore safe from serious crimes.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Again, even in their survey, public support for the death penalty was very high − 70% of the respondents were in favour.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But asked specifically what the penalty should be for intentional murder, trafficking in illegal drugs and discharging a firearm, the proportion in favour of the death penalty was even higher, ranging from 86% to 92%.

sections.label: DRC community-based programme outcomes
sections.summary: Since 1995, 15,000 DRC inmates have gone through the community-based programme with an 85% completion rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Since 1995, 15,000 DRC inmates have gone through the community-based programme with an 85% completion rate.

sections.label: Rehabilitation programmes for drug abusers
sections.summary: Under-21s get six months non-residential counselling; moderate-risk go to Community Rehabilitation Centre; ACE is a three-month programme for young drug abusers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If they are below the age of 21, they undergo counselling and casework management for a period of six months, and that is non-residential.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If they are of moderate risk, they are then sent to the Community Rehabilitation Centre.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They started operations in 2014 and that allows them to continue with their education and employment in the day with minimal disruption.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Even in there, we have split them into low risk, moderate risk and high risk with different types of treatment for the three categories.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We also started the Anti-Drug and Counselling Engagement or ACE, programme which was started last year for young drug abusers who have confessed to drug abuse but, for one reason or another, they have tested negative in the urine test.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This is a three-month programme and includes counselling and we equip them with skills to cope with their addictions.

sections.label: Strong stance on drug issues
sections.summary: The speaker says a strong stance is important in dealing with drug issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
sentences.text: Mr Kok, that would be out of order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
sentences.text: I think I did articulate in my speech that I do think that a strong stance is important in dealing with drug issues.

sections.label: People falling through social nets
sections.summary: The speaker clarifies it was not a critique of the system, noting some people fall through the nets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
sentences.text: I want to clarify that it was not a statement to critique the system that we have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
sentences.text: However, we have heard in the House quite a lot of times that even with all the social nets that we have put in, all the systems that we have put in, there will be people who have fallen through the nets.

sections.label: Importance of rehabilitative work
sections.summary: The speaker says rehabilitative work is important to help abusers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
sentences.text: What I am concerned is then, in the end, how can we help these abusers and that is why rehabilitative work, for me, is so important.

sections.label: Basis for socio-economic drug link
sections.summary: The speaker asks on what basis the socio-economic gap leads people to drugs, and notes a difference on the death penalty.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: My particular point was on what basis do you conclude that it is the social economic gap that leads some people to go into drugs?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But that is a discussion we can have some other time.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I note your difference in philosophy on the death penalty.

sections.label: Cocktailed drugs and Internet trafficking
sections.summary: The speaker proposes calibrating drug trafficking punishment for cocktailed drugs, flexible scheduling, and a new offence for Internet trafficking and recruiting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: My first suggestion is to calibrate the punishment of drug trafficking to take into account the harmfulness of cocktailed drugs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The consequences of a cocktailed drug can be more devastating to the drug user.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: It is for this reason that I suggested that the First Schedule be flexible enough to deal with the influx of new psycho-active substances and that the move from the Fifth Schedule to the First Schedule be prompt enough to frame a drug trafficking charge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Thirdly, Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan and Mr Alex Yam highlighted the need to stem the "route" of drugs being shipped in through the Internet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: This is why I proposed that a new offence be created with an enhanced punishment regime to tackle trafficking and recruiting through the Internet.

sections.label: Arrests of young drug abusers
sections.summary: The top line shows drug abusers arrested aged 20 to 29 reached 1,000 and over in 2015 and 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The top bright blue line snaking out at the top, way above the rest − that is what we should be concerned about.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: That line shows that the number of drug abusers arrested from between 20 and 29 years of age hit the 1,000 mark and over in 2015 and 2016.

sections.label: Staff recovered from drug dependence
sections.summary: The organisation is staffed mostly by recovered drug dependents, and a 2006 report said three quarters of previous users maintain sobriety.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: It is staffed mostly by those who have recovered from drug dependence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: It was reported in 2006 that three quarters of the previous users maintain sobriety.

sections.label: SANA anonymous live chat service
sections.summary: The Singapore Anti-Narcotics Association launched an anonymous live chat service on its talk2sana online portal last month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: A good local initiative is Singapore Anti-Narcotics Association's anonymous live chat service on its talk2sana online portal launched just last month.

sections.label: Preventive education against pro-drug culture
sections.summary: Mr Pritam Singh emphasised preventive education to deter a pro-drug culture, and the speaker notes bipartisan support for this collective battle.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Mr Pritam Singh emphasised the need for preventive education to deter the pro-drug culture from embedding itself here.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: It is significant that we have bipartisan support for this important, collective battle against a pro-drug culture.

sections.label: Youth survey on parental conversations
sections.summary: A 2013 survey showed 96.5% of youths whose parents spoke to them about drugs were deterred, but less than half had such conversations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The National Council Against Drug Abuse Youth Perception Survey in 2013 showed that while "96.5% of youths whose parents had spoken to them about drugs and drug abuse reported that those conversations have deterred them from taking drugs", only "less than half of the youths had conversations with their parents on drugs and drug abuse." This battle for the mindshare of young Singaporeans is not something we can under-estimate.

sections.label: Burden of proof and safeguards
sections.summary: The speaker says convictions are not meted out when investigations do not meet the Courts' burden of proof, citing Harven vs Public Prosecutor, and is open to more safeguards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: With regard to the insightful point raised by Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, I would respond that where the investigations do not meet the standards required by the Courts to meet the burden of proof, then the conviction is not meted out.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: This was so in the recent case of Harven vs Public Prosecutor decided just two weeks ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Two Judges in the Court of Appeal found the burden of proof was not met − Justice Chao Hick Tin delivering the majority decision; Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon concurring.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: One judge, Justice Tay Yong Kwang found it was met.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Developing the ethos behind Asst Prof Mahdev's points, I am open to further safeguards, such as having three judges sit at first instance for capital trials and five judges sitting in the Court of Appeal for all capital appeals.

sections.label: Mandatory death penalty deterrent
sections.summary: The speaker quotes DPM Teo that the mandatory death penalty deters traffickers, and says it is not wise to go soft against traffickers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: As Deputy Prime Minister Teo mentioned in the 2012 Misuse of Drugs Amendment (MDA) debate, and I quote, "We know that the mandatory death penalty has a deterrent effect because drug traffickers deliberately try to keep the amounts they carry to below the capital punishment threshold." So, for these principled reasons, in addition to the practical reasons that I have laid out, I do not think it wise, for the sake of the innocent victims, to go soft against traffickers.

sections.label: Addict began drugs at 13
sections.summary: In the DRC, one addict shared that he started consuming drugs when he was 13 years of age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In the DRC, one addict shared with me that he started consuming drugs when he was 13 years of age.

sections.label: Tough laws and rehabilitation
sections.summary: The speaker says loosening laws will make innocent families suffer, and Singapore must hold tough laws against traffickers, rehabilitation and prevention of a drug-tolerant culture.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Loosen the laws, multitudes of innocent families will suffer.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: What we must hold today is a crucial line − tough laws against drug traffickers; investing in the rehabilitation of drug addicts and preventing a drug-tolerant culture from being established in Singapore.
